completion_definition: Completed means the initial curated cross-reference pass: the source verse and every listed target passage were read in the pinned Saints-Translation English records, and each retained pair has a specific explanation. It does not mean every possible biblical connection has been exhausted, or independent scholarly approval.

editorial_notes.note: Retain Elishah in both supplied Japheth/Javan lists and Cainan in both supplied Shem and Arphaxad contexts. Cross-references do not remove or harmonize these differing placements.

The available Chronicles text contains no separate 1:11-16 or 1:18-23 units. Only actual available units are used. English forms such as Kitians/Kittians, Regma/Raamah, Sala/Shelah and Ragau/Reu remain distinct in their quoted sources.

Nimrod remains a giant hunter before the Lord in the supplied text. No claim that before means rebellion, or that Nimrod built the later tower, is added. Dasem is retained and the great-city clause is not independently resolved.
The nations comparison retains Deuteronomy's angels-of-God wording without forcing a traditional number of peoples or mapping the genealogies onto modern racial identities.
Language settings and comprehension are compared thematically. Acts is not described as explicitly quoting Babel or declaring a reversal of Genesis 11:1.

The descent-and-seeing parallel preserves the supplied Sodom wording about being brought to an end according to the cry; a familiar alternate formulation about what the people have done was removed during peer QA.

Luke and Chronicles links establish corresponding genealogical positions only. They do not corroborate Genesis's ages, unnamed children or death notices. The combined Arphaxad/Cainan material remains within the original 11:13 anchor.

Do not merge the ancestor Nahor with Terah's son of the same name, Haran the deceased man with Harran the destination, or Iscah with Sara. Sara is the supplied name here and changes to Sarah at17:15. Acts7 and Nehemiah9 supply retrospective divine-action perspectives; no forced reconstruction of Terah's or Abram's birth years is imposed.

editorial_notes.note: Acts places the initial appearance before residence at Haran and narrates movement after the father's death. The records preserve its presentation alongside Genesis rather than imposing a new chronological harmonization.

The supplied Genesis says all the tribes of the earth in Abram; later texts speak of nations or families and, in Acts, the seed. These are labelled explicit reuse and interpretation without replacing the supplied English wording.
The connections concern Shechem and patriarchal acts there. The oak and the later terebinth are not asserted to be the same individual tree or parcel.
The supplied text says wilderness. No alternate Negev wording, precise geographical reconstruction or modern travel itinerary is inserted.

The later wife-and-sister episodes in Genesis 20 and 26 are narrative parallels. The comparison does not identify their rulers as one historical person, approve the deception, or claim identical circumstances. Sara and Sarah labels remain as supplied.
The family term brother is read alongside Genesis 12:5, which explicitly identifies Lot as Abram's brother's son. No biological brother relationship is substituted.
The supplied Genesis uses sand of the earth. Sirach 44:21 uses dust and stars; the related multitude imagery is retained with its own wording rather than made an exact verbal quotation.

The supplied king names, nations, giants, Ommaeans, rulers of Amalek, Salt Sea and itinerary remain intact. No modern identification of kings, reconstructed campaign route or resolution of possible chronological/geographical questions is claimed.

The account says the kings fled and fell into bitumen pits, and later mentions the king of Sodom meeting Abram. The retained links do not infer a death, an escape mechanism or a resolved identity question.
The supplied text repeatedly names horses. The records do not silently replace that reading with goods or a different textual stream's spoils terminology.
Man from beyond and Aunan are preserved from the supplied English. The record does not substitute Hebrew as a new lexical finding or normalize Aunan to another edition's proper name.

Melchizedek links follow the actual priesthood, blessing and tenth-giving reuse in Psalms and Hebrews. No Eucharistic interpretation is added merely from the loaves and wine, and Hebrews' theological claims are identified as that text's interpretation.
The shared household-born servant category does not establish that the later circumcision group contains exactly the same three hundred and eighteen individuals.

editorial_notes.note: The supplied reading names Masek, the slave woman born in Abram's house, and Damascus Eliezer. The review does not silently substitute the familiar steward-only wording or resolve the source's household syntax.
The Hebrews link compares divine assurance of promise. The oath discussed there is not claimed to be a quotation of Genesis 15; the surrounding Hebrews quotation recalls the later Abrahamic oath.

The birds requested for the covenant scene are distinguished from birds descending on the divided bodies. The source says Abram sat down with them at 15:11; drove them away is not imported from another edition.
Not dividing the bird is a particular ritual-handling comparison. It does not equate the covenant scene with later Sinai burnt-offering legislation.

Genesis's four-hundred-year affliction prediction and Exodus's four hundred and thirty years of residence in both Egypt and Canaan remain distinct. No harmonized chronology or textual-critical resolution is asserted.

Paul explicitly interprets the two women allegorically as covenants. Links are labelled later reuse and interpretation; the Genesis narrative is not claimed to state that allegory or give a new general prescription of slavery.
The actual opposite-all-his-brothers wording is linked to Genesis 25:18. No modern ethnic or political identification is added, and wilderness residence is not equated with every conflict phrase.

The supplied well and place labels are retained: The Well Where I Saw Before Me, Well of the Vision, and Form of God. Related seeing-and-naming comparisons do not claim new Hebrew etymological or geographical verification.
The supplied divine self-identification is I am your God. The review does not replace it with Almighty or claim a newly collated divine-name reading.
Romans quotes the name explanation in 17:5. The link from 17:4 is labelled reuse and interpretation of the multinational promise, not an exact quotation of that individual verse.

The eighth-day clause in Genesis is preserved. The Exodus comparison retains its angel, circumcision statement and ambiguous pronouns; the review does not identify an unstated threatened person or replace its wording with a bridegroom-of-blood formula.

The supplied Sara-to-Sarah distinction remains. In 17:16 the later blessing pronoun is him, the promised child; it is not silently changed to her. Nehemiah's supplied Abraam spelling likewise remains in the target evidence.
Genesis reports Abraham's laughter; Romans presents his faith in the promise. Both statements are retained without substituting a psychological diagnosis or erasing either account.
The promised twelve nations are compared with the later twelvefold descendant record. Variant supplied name spellings in Genesis and Chronicles are preserved rather than normalized.
The physical covenant sign and Colossians' circumcision-not-made-by-hands interpretation remain distinguished. Genesis is not claimed to mention baptism.

God, three men and later two angels are the supplied narrative labels. No new identification of the three visitors with distinct divine persons is asserted. Hebrews 13:2 is a qualified hospitality allusion, not an explicit naming of Abraham or Lot.
Sarah's my lord refers to her husband in the supplied inward speech. The Peter link concerns that designation and does not claim a word-for-word quotation of the whole Genesis verse.

The supplied Greek-based text asks whether they are being brought to an end according to the cry. Its wording is retained; the review does not replace it with another edition's formulation or settle questions about divine knowledge.
The declining fifty-to-ten appeals are kept distinct. Jeremiah concerns Jerusalem and one person doing justice. Conditional promises are not reported as though Sodom was in fact spared.

The source reports a hostile sexual demand against guests. Jude's other flesh wording is retained as a later interpretation without resolving every phrase or making claims about modern identity groups.
The hosts' offers of women are reported actions, not divine commands or endorsements. Genesis does not say Lot's offer was carried out; the later Gibeah outcome is not imported into Sodom.

The source says sons-in-law who had taken his daughters, and later they were troubled. These are not silently rewritten as betrothed sons-in-law or Lot lingered. The review does not harmonize the daughters' status by adding unreported family members.
Wisdom's righteous fugitive, Five Cities and salt pillar are linked as particular later recollections. No new archaeological location or evidentiary claim is made.

The absence of any man upon the earth is the older daughter's reported claim. It is not adopted as the narrator's assertion of worldwide extinction. The account's description of the father's unawareness is preserved.
The kinship prohibition is a later legal comparison, not a legal speech attributed to the daughters or a claim that the Genesis narrator explicitly issues that command in this scene.

The supplied Deuteronomy 2:9 has the land name Seir while addressing the Moabites and sons of Lot. That reading is not silently changed to another edition's Ar; the retained link concerns descent from Lot, not reconstructed territorial boundaries.
Genesis names the ancestor Amman and the people Ammanites, while Deuteronomy uses Ammon. Both English forms are retained and linked by the stated Lot ancestry rather than normalized away.

findings.problem: The rationale paraphrases the Sodom target as seeing what people have done. This supplied reading specifically asks whether they are being brought to an end according to their cry, so the familiar alternate formulation should not replace it.
findings.recommended_rationale: Both scenes describe the Lord coming down to see in a city-judgment setting. The supplied Sodom wording concerns whether they are being brought to an end according to the cry.
findings.action: Retain the literary parallel and revise its explanation; do not change either source passage.

findings.problem: Genesis 11:1 itself presents shared speech, not yet the subsequent loss of mutual understanding. The current rationale reaches ahead to that later problem rather than stating the direct difference between these two settings.
findings.recommended_rationale: Genesis opens with one shared language; Acts describes diverse languages spoken and understood by their hearers. The comparison concerns the narratives' linguistic settings rather than an explicit quotation of Genesis 11:1.
findings.action: Retain the thematic comparison; this wording more directly grounds it in the selected source verse.
